articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) of the U.S. Department of the Treasury announced the issuance of an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026.
This amendment updates previous guidance concerning transactions involving Iran, reflecting ongoing adjustments to U.S. sanctions policy.
Specific details of the amendments were not immediately released but are expected to clarify permissible activities under the Iranian Transactions and Sanctions Regulations (ITSR).

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals Linked to North Korea and DRC
body: OFAC announced new designations targeting individuals and entities connected to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) on October 28, 2026.

The North Korea-related designations include Russian and North Korean nationals linked to LIMITED LIABILITY COMPANY ALIS, CHINYONG INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY COOPERATION COMPANY, and FIRST FINANCIAL AND TECHNICAL DEVELOPMENT CENTER, with some entries listing digital currency addresses on Ethereum and TRON.

The DRC-related additions include Rwanda's Ministry of Defence and Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a Kigali-based financial institution, extending restrictions that can affect financial institutions and cross-border transactions.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for $1.5 Million Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider, has agreed to a $1,529,685 settlement with OFAC for nine apparent violations of U.S. sanctions targeting Russia.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and services from the United States to Joint Stock Company Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer majority-owned by a designated Russian state-owned company.
OFAC determined that the violations were egregious but voluntarily self-disclosed, emphasizing the importance of sanctions-related diligence in acquisitions and oversight of foreign operations.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Reporting
body: OFAC amended 11 of its Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC on October 26, 2026.
The revisions, part of an ongoing review of published guidance, clarify distinctions between blocking and rejecting transactions, handling blocked funds, and reporting obligations.

Key updates include instructions for reporting through the OFAC Reporting System (ORS) and expanded descriptions of supporting documentation required for initial blocking and rejected-transaction reports.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Sanctions Law Center

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New General Licenses and Amends FAQs for Iran and Russia, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations
body: OFAC announced Iran-related designations, Belarus and North Korea designations removals, and the issuance of Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended Frequently Asked Questions on October 21, 2026.
This multifaceted action indicates a recalibration of sanctions measures across several programs, including both new restrictions and relaxations.
The specific details of the designations, removals, and general licenses were not immediately available but are expected to impact various sectors and entities involved with these regions.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements PAIPA Designations and Associated General Licenses
body: OFAC announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) and the issuance of associated General Licenses on October 19, 2026.
These actions aim to combat intellectual property theft and protect American innovation by targeting individuals and entities involved in such illicit activities.
The accompanying General Licenses are intended to mitigate unintended consequences and provide authorizations for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question on October 16, 2026.
This amendment reflects ongoing adjustments to U.S. policy towards Venezuela, potentially impacting certain sectors or transactions.
The updated guidance aims to provide clarity for stakeholders engaging in activities related to Venezuela under the existing sanctions framework.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals Related to Iran and Cuba, Issues New General Licenses
body: OFAC announced Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation, alongside the issuance of new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions on October 15, 2026.
These actions underscore the U.S. government's continued pressure on both Iran and Cuba through targeted sanctions.
The new and amended General Licenses and FAQs are intended to provide guidance and potential authorizations for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under these sanctions programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: OFAC announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation on October 14, 2026.
This action indicates a potential easing of sanctions on a specific entity or individual previously targeted under the Venezuela sanctions program.
Such removals often follow a review of the designated party's activities and compliance with U.S. sanctions policy objectives.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: OFAC announced new Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations on October 13, 2026.
These designations target individuals and entities involved in illicit drug trafficking and terrorism financing, aiming to disrupt their networks and financial operations.
The actions reinforce the U.S. government's commitment to combating these threats globally through economic sanctions.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Fined $1.5 Million by OFAC for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle its potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

The violations involved the export of networking equipment and services to a Russian defense manufacturer, Joint Stock Company Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), which was majority-owned by a designated Russian state-owned company.

OFAC determined the violations were egregious but voluntarily self-disclosed, highlighting the importance of robust sanctions compliance, especially in mergers and acquisitions and oversight of foreign subsidiaries.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11.6 Million Over Sanctions Breaches
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to pay $11,662,930 to settle potential civil liability for 475 apparent violations of multiple OFAC sanctions programs, including those targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Myanmar, Somalia, narcotics trafficking, and global terrorism.

The violations, occurring between September 2021 and April 2025, involved approximately $14.83 million in transactions and were attributed to deficiencies in payment screening, delayed sanctions watchlist updates, and human errors.
OFAC determined the violations were non-egregious but largely not voluntarily self-disclosed, and the settlement reflects no reduction from the base penalty.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Fined $175,015 by OFAC for Illicit Drug Trade Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based freight forwarder, has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle potential civil liability for four apparent violations of the Illicit Drug Trade Sanctions Regulations and six violations of the Reporting, Procedures and Penalties Regulations.

The violations stemmed from arranging a shipment for a U.S. customer of a sugar-packet filling machine from a Chinese firm, Youli Technology Development Co., Ltd., which was on the SDN List for narcotics-related activities.
OFAC criticized Pegasus for screening too late and for failing to respond properly to an OFAC subpoena, emphasizing the need for robust and timely sanctions screening beyond just name matching.

articles.headline: Individual Settles with OFAC for $1.4 Million for Sanctions Violations
body: An unnamed individual has agreed to pay $1,427,230 to settle potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions.
This significant penalty underscores OFAC's enforcement against individuals who breach U.S. sanctions regulations.
The details of the specific violations were not publicly disclosed, but such high penalties often involve egregious conduct or substantial transaction values.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems Fined $60,764 by OFAC for Iran Sanctions Breaches
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc., a Wisconsin-based manufacturer, has agreed to pay $60,764 to settle its potential civil liability for eight apparent violations of OFAC sanctions on Iran.

The violations occurred when its Italian subsidiary, Dini Argeo S.r.l., exported weighing equipment to Iran through a distributor in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) between June 2019 and November 2021, with knowledge of the ultimate destination.

OFAC determined the case was non-egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed, but highlighted the company's failure to adequately explain and monitor compliance with indirect sales restrictions to its foreign subsidiary.

articles.headline: FTI Consulting, Inc. Pays $1.05 Million to Settle OFAC Violations
body: FTI Consulting, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,050,000 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions.
This settlement underscores the importance of compliance for consulting firms operating internationally, particularly when dealing with sanctioned jurisdictions or entities.
The specific nature of the violations was not detailed in the public announcement, but the substantial penalty indicates serious compliance shortcomings.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Fined $275 Million by OFAC for Iran Sanctions Violations
body: Adani Enterprises Limited (AEL), an India-headquartered multinational company, has agreed to pay $275,000,000 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions on Iran.

From November 2023 to June 2025, AEL purchased shipments of liquified petroleum gas (LPG) from a Dubai-based trader, causing U.S. financial institutions to process 32 U.S. dollar payments totaling approximately $192 million for Iranian-origin LPG.
OFAC determined the violations were egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed, citing AEL's reckless disregard for U.S. sanctions and failure to heed numerous red flags.

articles.headline: TradeStation Securities Fined $1.1 Million by OFAC for Sanctions Breaches
body: TradeStation Securities, Inc., a Florida-headquartered brokerage firm, has agreed to pay $1,110,661 to settle its potential civil liability for 481 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programs.

Between June 2021 and June 2022, TradeStation provided investment services to customers located in Iran, Syria, and the Crimea region of Ukraine, enabling them to execute securities-related transactions.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were non-egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed, emphasizing the importance for financial institutions to deploy testing mechanisms to ensure compliance tools are functioning as intended.

articles.headline: Individual Pays $3.7 Million to OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: An unnamed individual has agreed to pay $3,777,000 to settle potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions.
This substantial penalty, one of the largest against an individual, highlights OFAC's focus on enforcing sanctions against individuals engaged in illicit activities.
The details surrounding the specific violations were not publicly disclosed, but the amount suggests a high-value egregious transaction or a pattern of significant non-compliance.

articles.headline: IMG Academy Settles with OFAC for $1.7 Million Over Counternarcotics Sanctions Violations
body: IMG Academy, LLC, a Florida-based school and athletic training facility, has agreed to pay $1,720,000 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC counternarcotics sanctions.
Over five consecutive years, IMG Academy repeatedly transacted with two individuals sanctioned by OFAC due to their ties to a Mexican-based drug cartel.

OFAC determined the violations were non-egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed, emphasizing the importance for institutions across various sectors, including academic, to implement effective, risk-based controls to prevent sanctions violations.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
